articles.description:
perf_event_paranoid controls observability privilege, not process trust


Performance monitoring can expose more than instruction counts. It can sample execution, collect stack traces, observe kernel behavior, and provide timing information that helps an attacker understand a target. Linux exposes a system-wide knob that limits what an unprivileged process may measure: perf_event_paranoid.
The kernel documentation defines a useful scale. At -1, almost all events are open to all users. At 0 or higher, unprivileged users cannot use ftrace function tracepoints or raw tracepoints without CAP_PERFMON. At 1 or higher, CPU event access is restricted. At 2 or higher, kernel profiling is disallowed. The default is 2. A privileged process can still bypass the checks, so the setting is not a substitu…

Most agent payment setups have one guardrail: a per-payment limit. "Never pay more than $50."

Passive intermodulation is the specification that most often disappears from a component RFQ — and then reappears as a failed system test. A switch contact, a connector interface or a load can all behave as a weak nonlinear junction when two carriers are present.
Two tones at f₁ and f₂ passing through a nonlinearity produce products at mf₁ ± nf₂. The third-order terms 2f₁−f₂ and 2f₂−f₁ are the dangerous ones because they land close to the original carriers and can fall inside the receiver band. A typical test applies two 20 W tones and measures the third-order product in dBc; a well-built path might be −150 dBc or better, while a dirty or loose interface can be 30–40 dB worse.

Event Driven Approach
We can use AWS to create a solution that:
1. Stores our documents in Amazon S3.
2. Captures document events using Amazon EventBridge.
3. Processes events asynchronously using Amazon SQS.
4. Extracts, detects and processes document changes using AWS Lambda.
5. Creates embeddings and enables smart document search using Amazon Bedrock.
6. Stores our document embeddings in a vector database.
7. 
This ensures that only the specific document that has changed needs to be processed.
Engineering Challenges
It is interesting to think about how we can make sure this is reliable. We need to consider handling duplicate events, failures, document versions, removal of documents and incomplete sync.
Why it Matters
Whilst creating a RAG application is easy to do, creating a reliable, accurate and scalable knowledge base is very interesting.

A technology project can look impressive in a demo and still fail when real users depend on it.
Before choosing AI, blockchain, or a conventional database, I would ask three questions.
First, can we explain where the data comes from and who is allowed to modify it?
Second, can someone independently verify an important result?
Third, what happens when the system fails, an input is incorrect, or a user needs a correction?
These questions influence architecture, testing, access control, monitoring, and maintenance.
For blockchain projects, immutability does not guarantee that the original information is true. For AI projects, fluent output does not guarantee accuracy.
Trustworthy software needs evidence, accountability, and clear limitations.

The concrete detail I'm proud of: the template generates the admin and app keys at deploy time with openssl rand inside the start script, so nobody ever commits a config with default secrets. Federation (ActivityPub) is enabled out of the box, which is the part most people botch — the site and open federation flags plus a proper instance domain are the difference between a blog that talks to the fediverse and one that silently doesn't.
What it costs the operator: SQLite works fine and is the zero-config default, but the moment you want more than one replica or real concurrent writes, you're migrating to Postgres, and WriteFreely's schema doesn't make that a one-liner. I documented the migration path in the README rather than hiding it. Running your own instance also means you're the moderator — federation brings spam registrations, and the blocklist is on you.
It's a small thing — a template, not a product — but it removes the three steps where everyone I watched quit.

articles.description:
Voice memos, WhatsApp audio you saved, screen recordings of a call: on an iPhone almost all of it ends up as M4A or MOV. That's fine inside Apple's apps, but the moment you need to upload a recording to a form, a car stereo, an older MP3 player or a podcast host that wants MP3, it gets awkward. A few practical notes from dealing with this a lot:
1. Get the file out of the Voice Memos app first. Open the memo, tap the three dots, then "Save to Files". Now it's a normal .m4a file you can pick from any browser upload button.
2. Don't go above the source quality. Voice Memos records AAC at roughly 64-128 kbps depending on your "Audio Quality" setting. Exporting that as a 320 kbps MP3 only makes the file bigger. 128 kbps is plenty for speech; 96 kbps mono is fine for meeting notes.
3. For videos, you only want the audio track. Screen recordings and camera videos are MOV files. Converting them straight to MP3 drops the video and usually shrinks the file by 90% or more.
4. Trim silence before converting. Cutting the dead air at the start in the Voice Memos editor saves a second re-encode later.
5. Rename before sharing. "2026-11-14 client call.mp3" beats "New Recording 47.mp3" when it lands in someone else's inbox.
For the conversion itself you don't need an app: we wrote up how to turn iPhone voice memos into MP3 straight from Safari, and the M4A to MP3 converter it uses runs in the browser with no sign-up. (Disclosure: it's our project.)
What do you usually need MP3 for these days: uploads, car audio, or something else?

articles.description:
This article was prepared with AI assistance and reviewed by its author.
A memory feature needs an acceptance test, not just a successful retrieval demo.
Start with one small task whose answer you can check. Record its inputs, expected answer and permissions before enabling memory. Then try five cases:
Recall: save a useful project fact, start a new session and check whether the agent retrieves the right source.
Correction: replace that fact with a newer decision. Check that the agent uses the correction and exposes the old note as superseded.
Missing context: ask about an unstored detail. The agent should expose the gap instead of treating a guess as remembered evidence.
Isolation: repeat the question in a separate test workspace. Check that another workspace's private notes do not appear.
Deletion: remove the test note and check retrieval again, including any application cache involved in the workflow.
Run the same task without memory as a baseline. Keep a small results table with the case, expected result, retrieved evidence, actual answer and pass or failure. Repeat after changing extraction, retrieval or retention behavior.
This is a proposed evaluation procedure, not a benchmark result. It tests whether memory helps the particular workflow while preserving correction, permissions and deletion controls.

1/λ = R (1/n_f² − 1/n_i²), where R = 1.0968 × 10⁷ m⁻¹. Electrons falling to n = 2 give the visible Balmer series. Energy levels are Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV.
const R = 1.0968e7;
const nm = (nf, ni) => 1e9 / (R * (1 / nf ** 2 - 1 / ni ** 2));

for (const ni of [3, 4, 5, 6]) console.log(ni, '->2', nm(2, ni).toFixed(1), 'nm');

These match the measured Balmer lines. The same function gives 121.6 nm for the Lyman 2 → 1 line (ultraviolet) and 1876 nm for the Paschen 4 → 3 line (infrared), so only the Balmer series is visible.
The 3 → 2 jump releases E₃ − E₂ = −1.51 − (−3.40) = 1.89 eV. The wavelength is λ = 1240 / E nm = 1240 / 1.89 ≈ 656 nm, the same red line.
Its lines end on n = 2 and have energies of about 1.9 to 3.0 eV, which fall in the visible range. The Lyman lines are more energetic (ultraviolet) and the Paschen lines less (infrared).

The speed a satellite needs to stay in orbit and the speed needed to escape Earth are linked by one number, √2. You can check it in a few lines of JavaScript, and the same code gives the period of the ISS and of a geostationary satellite. (I build PractiSci, which has a free satellite-orbits lab.)
Orbital speed at height h: v = √(GM/(R + h)). Escape speed: v_esc = √(2GM/(R + h)). Orbital period: T = 2π√((R + h)³/GM).
const G = 6.674e-11, Me = 5.972e24, Re = 6.371e6;
const orbitV = (h) => Math.sqrt(G * Me / (Re + h));
const period = (h) => 2 * Math.PI * Math.sqrt((Re + h) ** 3 / (G * Me));
const escape = (h) => Math.sqrt(2 * G * Me / (Re + h));

The ratio escape/orbital is 1.4142 at every height, which is √2. That is why a satellite already has about 70% of the speed it would need to leave Earth altogether.
Its period must equal one sidereal day, 23.93 h. Solving T = 2π√(r³/GM) for r gives r ≈ 42,164 km from the centre of the Earth, which is 35,786 km above the surface. Then the satellite stays over the same point on the equator.
No. It cancels, so a tiny satellite and a space station at the same height have the same speed.
They are in free fall around the Earth, not beyond gravity. Gravity at 400 km is still about 89% of its surface value.

articles.author: Kato Emmanuel

I've been building a product at work for 6 months. Every line of code was written by AI. It still isn't finished.
People keep telling me AI makes building software easy. That hasn't been my experience.
AI is very fast at writing code. But typing code was never the slow part. The slow part is deciding what to build, keeping the design coherent across hundreds of prompts, and remembering why you chose something three weeks ago. The AI doesn't carry that for you. It will also happily generate two pieces that quietly contradict each other, then help you debug the mess it made.
Fast code means fast problems. A big share of these 6 months has gone into reviewing, untangling, re-prompting and fixing things that looked fine when they were generated.
I'm not going back to working without it. It's a great tool. But it changed where the work sits for me: less typing, more judgment. Design, review, debugging, trade-offs.
My own project tells the same story. Publlsh, the tool I'm posting this from, is built the same way. I started it in February, about 9 months ago, and it's still not complete.
So no, I don't think AI replaces engineers. If anything, the people who understand how systems fit together get the most out of it.
Anyone else building with mostly AI-generated code? I'd like to hear what caught you off guard.

Who is open? — lead, discovery, proposal sent, waiting, active, won, lost


When did I last touch them? — a date, not a vibe


What is the next visible action? — one verb: send proposal, nudge, send invoice, schedule kickoff, mark lost
I keep it boring on purpose: a Clients list, a Pipeline board (Lead → Discovery → Proposal → Won / Active / Lost), and an Invoices table (Draft → Sent → Due → Overdue → Paid). Notion works. A Markdown table works. A spreadsheet works. The tool matters less than looking at it once a week before you open chat.
You can steal the shape today: make three columns (name / last touch / next action), dump every half-alive lead into it, and set one 15-minute Friday review. No kit required.

A successful smart contract deployment is not the same as a production-ready application.
Before release, I would want the team to demonstrate five things:
Network identity. Confirm the expected chain ID, deployment address, contract bytecode, and configuration.


Reproducibility. Show that another developer can repeat the deployment and verification process in a controlled environment.


Failure handling. Test RPC timeouts, failed transactions, delayed confirmations, and unavailable external services.


Access control. Verify privileged operations, key management, permission boundaries, and recovery procedures.


Data integrity. Document how off-chain information is collected, validated, and connected to on-chain records.



These checks do not guarantee security. They make important assumptions visible and create a starting point for independent testing.

articles.description:
My name is Hrithic Rajpurohit, and I work on the engineering team at Produsa Labs. We built Produsa, an AI website builder made for India, so I should tell you that before I describe how the build pipeline works.
A website build is not one task. Research, brand, copy, layout, code and a final check all ask different things of a model. If the whole job goes through a single model, the writing, the design sense and the engineering quality all settle at whatever that model is average at.
Produsa instead sends each job to the model that does it best. The ones we use are Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, xAI/Grok and Kimi. We have not published a map of which model takes which step, so I will not invent one here. The useful part is the idea: pick the model for the job, not one model for the whole product.
We also added a second, separate pass. After a page is written and designed, a different AI reviews it against a written design rulebook. The first pass can look finished and still miss the brief, repeat a layout, or drift from the brand. That review only works if the rulebook is specific enough to fail. A vague "make it look good" rule just gets a yes.
What I would tell another team doing this: write the bar down before you hook up the reviewer. If the only standard lives in someone's head, the review pass has nothing firm to argue with.
If you have tried a reviewer model on generated UI or copy, I am curious what you put in the rulebook, and what it still lets through.
This article was drafted with AI assistance and then checked by me. I can stand behind the facts above.

articles.description:
Disclosure: I run PickAPlugin, an independent catalog of ChatGPT and Codex plugins. This is adapted from our guide on the same topic.
There are basically three ways a plugin gets onto your machine: the built-in directory, a GitHub repo that ships a marketplace, or a folder you made yourself. Here's each one.
In the Codex app or ChatGPT desktop app, open Plugins, search, open the plugin and hit install. In the CLI, start codex and type /plugins. Plugins in the OpenAI tab are the ones OpenAI curates, so this is the low-risk route.
Most community plugins live in a repo that has a .agents/plugins/marketplace.json (or the older .claude-plugin/marketplace.json). You add the repo as a marketplace once, then install by name:
codex plugin marketplace add owner/repo
codex plugin list
codex plugin add plugin-name@marketplace-name

The marketplace name comes from the name field in that repo's marketplace.json, and codex plugin list shows it.
Point it at the repo, not the raw marketplace.json URL. The command clones a git repo, so a raw file link fails with a 404.
Put the plugin in ./plugins/my-plugin (repo) or ~/.codex/plugins/my-plugin (personal), then list it in .agents/plugins/marketplace.json with "source": {"source": "local", "path": "./plugins/my-plugin"}. Restart the app and it shows up.
Community plugins can bundle hooks, MCP servers and shell commands. Spend two minutes on the repo: when was the last commit, what does .mcp.json start, are there hooks.
Where do plugins get installed? Into ~/.codex/plugins/cache/MARKETPLACE/PLUGIN/VERSION/. Local plugins use the version local.
How do I remove one? codex plugin remove plugin-name@marketplace, or uninstall from the Plugins view in the app.
Why a 404 on marketplace add? Usually a raw marketplace.json URL. Give it the repo instead.
The full guide, with an install command finder, is at https://pickaplugin.com/guides/install-codex-plugin

articles.author: Sudhir Prasad
articles.description:
There's so much more to a company than its LinkedIn profile, employee count or funding announcements. 
Its engineering ecosystem can tell you what it's building, what technologies it's adopting, what it's moving away from and where potential opportunities might exist.
A few places worth exploring - 
GitHub
What are they building? Which repositories are active? What frameworks and technologies are they using? Are they contributing to open source? What direction is their engineering team moving towards?
Package registries
Look at npm, PyPI and other package ecosystems. What are they publishing, installing, maintaining or depending on? These can reveal a lot about their actual technology choices.
Docker Hub and container registries
What images are they pushing? What infrastructure are they running? Are they adopting new tools or changing their existing stack?
Engineering job openings
What roles are they hiring for? Are they looking for Kubernetes engineers, AI infrastructure specialists, DevOps engineers or people with experience in a particular technology?
Hiring often gives you a glimpse of what's coming next.
Developer communities
Look at Dev.to, Reddit, Stack Overflow, technical blogs and engineering discussions. What problems are they talking about? What tools are they evaluating? What are their developers experimenting with?
Technology adoption and migrations
Are they adopting a new technology? Moving away from an existing infrastructure? Replacing a solution? Building something internally?
These movements can tell you much more than a company description ever will.
The interesting part is that none of these signals, on their own, tells the complete story.
But when you start connecting them, you get a much better picture of what is happening inside a company.
And that's probably a much more interesting way to research an account than just looking at its LinkedIn profile.
Something worth exploring if you're in technical GTM.

We had all 6 of our new App Store listings rejected under guideline 4.3 since September, while updates to our 20 live apps passed review. Here is what 4.3 says, what we learned, and the check we now run before every submission.
4.3(a): "Don't create multiple Bundle IDs of the same app." Apple's example is a separate map app for every city; it wants one app with variations through in-app purchase.
4.3(b): "Don't submit apps that are indistinguishable from what's already widely available." It names dating, flashlight, sound effects, wallpaper, simple timers and fortune telling as well-established kinds that need "a meaningfully different or improved experience."
One app, not many bundle IDs.
Search the store for your exact name and core idea before you submit.
If you're in a named crowded category, say plainly what's different.
Compare against your own catalog. Near-copies of your other apps count.
Put the difference in the first lines of your description and subtitle.

Real output for the tool's built-in example listing.
We automated steps 2 and 4 as a free browser tool: 4.3 Radar (https://radar43.pages.dev/). It sends your app name and three keywords to Apple's public search, compares your listing in your browser, and gives a risk level with reasons. Your description isn't sent anywhere. It covers the US store's public search and text only; it can't predict App Review.
Disclosure: we built 4.3 Radar. There's an optional paid review; the check itself is free.
articles.title: Why Apple rejects apps under guideline 4.3, and a free check before you submit

結論からいうと、deciderというサイトには米国の映画メディアがありまして、そちらにはいろいろな意味で負けているのかもしれません。
「なんでDeciderなのにDeciderにならないんだ」みたいなことをずっと思ってはいましたよ。ただ、ルールもメカニズムもはっきりしたところが分からない。
どうやらグローバルで1つだと分かったときに「え、巨大サイトと争ってたの？」みたいな絵が見えてきて、その時の感想は、なんのこっちゃですよね。そちらがDeciderであるということは、うちは当然 Decider ではない。本当に？
あと余談とも言い切れない話として、カタカナのディサイダーではアイドルが活躍されております。明日のことは分からないのですが、今日はこの頃は当社はもう絶対に表示されなくなりましたよ。夏頃は出てたけどね。いまはアイドルと釣り具。
これは、ウイナー・テイクス・オールで当然ということなのでしょうか？
サイト名がフィッシングを防止するという少し違った役割を持つ点は理解するものの、法的な権利を阻害するような選択権を実効的に１社が持ってしまっている面には疑問があります。法制度が歪んでいるように見えます。
商標制度はそもそも（分野別に独占するとしても）重複は当然あることを前提とした制度であり、「ラベルは1つです」というルールを宣言することじたいが法制度と矛盾します。
しかも、日本語だったら日本しか使ってないから競合性が低いものの、英語が公用語の国はたくさんあるので、国家主権どうしが対立したら優劣の問題でもないでしょう。ここまで書いていて気づきましたが、日本国に頑張って欲しい話でもあるな。
冒頭に Decider, directly. というサイト名を書いたとおり、いま狙っているラベルはもう Decider じゃない。
たぶん、ディサイダーであれば取れるのかもしれないのですが、これだと日本から出られないサイトになってしまうので違う。
商標制度じたいは自社ブランドを識別するワードとして使用していないと権利が薄まってしまうので、使えないという制約を理解できないと同時に、使うことも課せられている。
さらに困ったことに、Decider, directly. を主張し続けているのですが、これがまた認識しない。bingにはサイト名ついたけどね。
たしかに、ドメイン文字列に一切 decider を入れてないんですよ。スターリーグのサイトだからね。ただ、ドメインで決まるとも言ってないじゃないか。
ここは確かに Decider を提供している株式会社スターリーグのドメインである star.careers だと確認したうえで Decider というラベルを付けるのが Google の仕事なわけですよ。確信が持てない、ではなくてね。確信が持てないのであれば、他のサイトにも Decider を付けたらダメという論も立つ。
いや、言いたいことは Decider から Decider のサイト名を剥奪してくれということでなくて、もはや同じラベルじゃないワードを選んで、商標権者が合理的に理解できるサイト名つけたら、暫定でもそれは付けなきゃダメなんじゃないの？ということです。
再登場させると、最近になってfaviconも表示されなくなり、もはやブランドの体裁がない状態です。継続使用による識別力の前提がありません。
いま、しつこくラベルを随所に表示するという、見ようによっては小細工を継続しており、どこかでは反映されるだろうと見ています。bingにはだいぶ前にサイト名ついたけどね。
ただ、faviconはあったものが消えたわけで、折に触れて消える程度のうたかた的存在なのかもしれないな、という見方も成立します。
要するに、Googleのサイトレベルのシグナルは、かなりバグ含みな感触を持っているのでさすがに直して欲しいと思います。
articles.title: サイト名がつかなくて困っているのだよ、Googleさん

articles.author: JSLab
articles.description:
JSLab feature notes: one docs page, explained. Today: Formatting.
Scratch code is written fast and formatted never. JSLab, a JavaScript & TypeScript scratchpad for macOS, formats with Prettier, so the mess you typed at speed can look like code before you paste it anywhere.
⌥⇧F (Format Code) formats the current tab. It's also in Actions → Format Code and the command palette.
const order={id:42,items:[{sku:"A-1",qty:2},{sku:"B-7",qty:1}],paid:true}
const total=order.items.reduce((sum,item)=>sum+item.qty,0)
total

One ⌥⇧F later:
const order = {
  id: 42,
  items: [
    { sku: "A-1", qty: 2 },
    { sku: "B-7", qty: 1 },
  ],
  paid: true,
};
const total = order.items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.qty, 0);
total;

The format lands as one undo step, and JSLab applies minimal edits instead of replacing the whole buffer, so your folds, scroll position and cursor stay where they were.
Two settings, both off by default:
Format on Run (Settings → General) formats before each run, unless you're typing.
Format on Save (Settings → Editor) formats when you save a file.
Settings → Formatting holds every Prettier option JSLab supports, with Prettier's usual defaults:



Setting
Default




Print Width
80


Tab Width
2


Semicolons
On


Single Quotes
Off


Trailing Commas
All


Arrow Parens
Always



Plus Use Tabs, Quote Props, JSX Single Quotes, Bracket Spacing and Bracket Same Line. Print Width goes from 20 to 320, and Tab Width from 1 to 16.
If Prettier can't parse the tab, the status bar says Couldn't format, with Prettier's message, and your code is left as it was. A format that takes too long is stopped and the formatter restarts, so a giant paste can't hang the editor.
JSLab launches Nov 15. The full page: https://js-lab.app/docs/formatting
articles.title: Prettier on demand, on run, on save

[10:41:02] change detected

articles.author: Quantooox
articles.description:
Anyone can show an impressive track record after the fact. The question is whether the predictions existed before the outcomes. We wanted a way to prove that, cheaply, without asking anyone to trust us.
Every night:
The day's scores are written to a CSV file, before the next market open.
The file's SHA-256 fingerprint goes into a ledger, with the publication time.
The file and the ledger are committed to git and pushed to a public repository.
The file is timestamped with OpenTimestamps, which anchors its hash in the Bitcoin blockchain.
A ledger row looks like this:
date,version,file,sha256,rows,published_at
2026-10-19,v1,scores/2026-10-19.csv,c657649932bf899f72043e60cad05f74527c9d6c22e51f7a44d57c79b2a1a560,99,2026-10-20T10:51:30+00:00

SHA-256: change a single character in the file and the fingerprint changes completely.
git: history is public; rewriting it shows up for anyone who cloned earlier.
OpenTimestamps: the strongest layer. The hash is committed into a Bitcoin transaction, so it proves the file
existed by that block's time, and it doesn't depend on GitHub or us. It's free.
One practical gotcha: git can normalise line endings on checkout, which changes the bytes and breaks the hash. A .gitattributes rule keeps the files byte-exact.
sha256sum track_record/scores/2026-10-19.csv     # compare with the ledger
ots verify track_record/scores/2026-10-19.csv.ots

It goes into a public corrections log. The original file stays as it was. Corrections are new entries, never edits.
Because "trust me" isn't evidence. With this, the scores either beat random picks over time or they don't, and nobody can quietly rewrite which.
From Quantooo Lab, the makers of quantooo.com, a free, open and educational quant lab: every formula, every test and every failure is public. See it here: https://quantooo.com/track-record
Educational, not investment advice.
articles.title: A track record nobody can edit: SHA-256, git and Bitcoin timestamps

articles.author: 冯智勇Geo
articles.description:
先说结论


处理一堆脏数据时，我现在更愿意先把模型能力、上下文和执行条件给足，而不是自己坐下来设计分类。尤其是大量杂乱文档的整理，真正困难的地方不是改几个标题、挪几个位置，而是要先理解所有内容，再判断它们应该怎样组织、哪些信息互相关联。
过去总觉得整理数据是简单劳动，用便宜模型就可以。实际效果不好，又以为问题在于自己没有先把结构设计清楚。现在重新想，这个判断可能一开始就错了：不是所有整理工作都适合用低成本模型做。数据越脏、越缺少明确规则，越可能需要更强的推理能力。

最近整理自己的 ChatGPT Space 资料库时，面对一大堆杂乱文档，常常不知道从哪里下手。文档多了，不只是内容需要修改，还涉及分类、归属、关联关系，以及不同资料应该如何一起维护。
我之前的想法很简单：让 AI 去做这些整理工作，应该不难，所以没有必要在模型和 Token 上花太多成本。结果整理出来的效果不理想。后来甚至开始反思，是不是应该先由自己确定整个目录架构，让 AI 按照人的分类去执行。
这个思路看起来很稳妥，却忽略了另一个可能性：如果交给 AI 的本来就是一件复杂的理解任务，我却一直用低配置的方式去做，那么问题未必出在分类方法上。
一份结构化、格式统一的数据，字段是什么意思、怎样归类、需要转换成什么样，往往都很明确。这样的工作交给脚本或者便宜模型就能处理，甚至不一定需要大模型。
但杂乱文档不是这样。它们可能来自不同时间、不同项目，表达方式不一致；有的内容是在记录过去的决定，有的是目前正在执行的规则，还有的只是一个没有展开的想法。AI 需要先判断每份材料是什么，再综合其他材料理解它的用途。
也就是说，干净数据通常是在执行规则；脏数据可能需要先发现规则、建立结构，再执行规则。后者看上去像整理杂物，实际上包含不少理解和推理。
以前恰恰在这种不确定性最高的地方节省模型能力，整理不好以后，又用自己的时间去弥补。
这次更重要的想法变化，是不再默认由人来设计分类架构。既然准备把资料库交给 AI 维护，那么目录应该怎么分、文档放在哪里、哪些内容应该关联，本来就可以是 AI 的工作。
人的输入可以很简单：这是一套什么资料，要整理到什么程度，哪些历史内容必须保留，最后希望怎样查找和使用。至于逐份阅读、提出分类、调整目录、建立链接、检查遗漏和冲突，都让 AI 去做。
我不需要一开始就看完所有文章，也不需要先替 AI 画好一张思维导图。等它整理出结果，再按需要检查结构和效果。结构仍然重要，只是设计和维护结构这件事，不必天然归人负责。
如果一个便宜模型需要反复提示、返工，最后还要人工检查大量内容，它的调用费用虽然低，整个任务未必便宜。
反过来，强模型在混乱资料的理解、归类和关系判断上，如果能够减少返工和人工介入，那么更高的 Token 成本反而可能是划算的。这里衡量的不是单次调用价格，而是从接收资料到整理完成，究竟花了多少资源和人的精力。
这也意味着模型选择应该跟着任务变化。结构稳定、规则明确以后，再把批量修改、格式转换等重复工作交给低成本模型或脚本；在最混乱、最需要判断的初始阶段，不必急着省。
当然，模型能力不是全部。即使用了最强的模型，如果只能看到一小部分文档、读不到关联资料，或者没有权限修改目录和链接，整理效果依然会受限制。
所以，我说的“把能力开到最大”，不只是切换模型，还包括让 AI 拿到完成任务所需的上下文、工具和权限。大量文档可以分批读、统一盘点，而不是受单次上下文容量限制，就误以为已经看全。
权限也不是毫无边界地允许破坏。像批量删除、覆盖原文这类可能造成损失的操作，应当有版本记录和可恢复的方式。让 AI 真正能干活，与保留必要的回滚能力并不矛盾。
这次整理资料，让我修正的不是某一套目录结构，而是评估 AI 能力的方法。
当 AI 的工作结果不理想时，过去容易马上认为：这件事还是要由人来设计、判断、处理。现在更值得先检查的是：模型是不是太弱？上下文是不是不完整？工具和权限是不是限制了它？是不是为了省 Token，反而把问题弄得更复杂？
把资源开足不保证每次都能成功，但至少可以避免一个常见误判：拿低配置下的表现，去判断 AI 原本能做到什么程度。
尤其面对一堆脏乱、没有现成结构的资料，我更愿意先让足够强的 AI 把事情做明白。等数据整理好了，再谈怎样降低成本。
articles.title: 整理脏数据，不要吝啬模型算力和 Token

시뮬레이션이 예측을 넘어서려면, 분자 속으로 들어가야 한다


The Generalist에 실린 심일리(Simile) 박준성 CEO 인터뷰를 읽고 밤새 잠을 설쳤다. 80억 인류 행동 85% 정확도 예측이라니—숫자만 보면 압도적이다. 하지만 개발자 관점에서 보자. 행동 로그와 클릭스트림으로 학습한 트랜스포머가 아무리 커도, 단백질이 어떻게 접히고, 효소가 어떻게 기질을 인식하며, 약물이 포켓에 어떻게 들어맞는지를 '이해'하고 있지는 않다. 가중치 공간에서의 상관관계일 뿐, 원자 단위의 인과관계는 아니다.  
2년 전, 내 팀은 알파폴드2(AlphaFold 2) 예측 구조로 타겟 단백질의 바인딩 포켓을 스크리닝하다가 벽에 부딪혔다. 정전기 표면도, 수소결합 네트워크, 입체 장애—이 모든 게 2D 뷰포트 위에서는 평평하게 납작해진다. PyMOL에서 돌리다가, ChimeraX에서 회전시키다가, 결국 OpenMM으로 200 ns 분자동역학을 돌려 앙상블을 뽑아내니 비로소 유연한 루프가 열리는 순간을 포착할 수 있었다. GPU 클러스터에서 8×A100으로 병렬 프리페어링을 걸고, MM‑PBSA로 자유에너지를 재계산하니 hit‑rate이 3 %에서 12 %로 뛰었다.  
그 경험이 말해준다. 정적 구조만으로는 ‘결합 가능하다’는 가설만 남고, 동적 앙상블과 양자‑역학 보정이 있어야 비로소 ‘결합한다’는 확신을 얻는다. 지금도 밤마다 트레이닝 로그를 보며, 다음 스텝에서 어떤 컨포머가 등장할지 상상한다.  
자세한 내용은 Simile 공식 사이트에서 확인해 보세요.

O que é


O Claude Code Game Studios é um sistema que transforma o Claude Code em um estúdio de desenvolvimento de jogos, utilizando 49 agentes de IA e 72 habilidades de fluxo de trabalho. O processo inicia com a descrição de um jogo; a ferramenta faz perguntas para definir a mecânica e a estética, cria um brief de design e constrói um protótipo jogável no navegador. O sistema inclui verificações automáticas para garantir que o jogo abra sem erros e que as funcionalidades do brief foram implementadas.
É voltado para desenvolvedores ou entusiastas que desejam criar jogos de forma iterativa. O sistema serve para quem quer transformar ideias simples em projetos reais, permitindo adicionar funcionalidades passo a passo, criar painéis de ajuste com controles deslizantes para valores do jogo e, eventualmente, converter o protótipo em um projeto web profissional com Vite e TypeScript. Também é útil para quem já possui um jogo e deseja importá-lo para aprimorá-lo.
Primeiro, instale os pré-requisitos: Git, Claude Code (via instalador nativo ou npm), Python 3 e Bash. Para testar e validar os jogos, é necessário ter o Chrome, Edge ou Chromium. Para transformar o protótipo em um projeto web completo, o Node.js é recomendado. Após a configuração, clone o repositório, abra o Claude Code e utilize o comando /prototype seguido da descrição da ideia do seu jogo para iniciar o desenvolvimento.
git clone https://github.com/Donchitos/Claude-Code-Game-Studios.git my-game
   cd my-game

articles.author: cendyandreoli
articles.description:
Brazil's central bank (Banco Central do Brasil) publishes the average revolving credit card rate for individuals as series 25477 in its SGS time-series service. The API is public, needs no key and returns JSON.
curl -s "https://api.bcb.gov.br/dados/serie/bcdata.sgs.25477/dados?formato=json&dataInicial=01/09/2025&dataFinal=30/09/2026"

Each row looks like {"data":"01/09/2026","valor":"15.29"}. The value is the monthly rate in percent, as a string, and the date is always day 01 of the month.
September 2026: 15.29% per month.
September 2025: 15.23% per month.
The monthly rate stayed between 14.90% (Jan 2026) and 15.44% (May 2025) over the last 24 months.
The API gives monthly only. The yearly rate is (1 + m)^12 - 1:
m = 0.1529
print(round(((1 + m) ** 12 - 1) * 100, 2))  # 451.44

R$ 1,000 left untouched for 12 months at that rate becomes about R$ 5,514 (1000 * 1.1529 ** 12). In Brazil, Law 14.690/2023 caps interest and fees at 100% of the original debt, so the real ceiling is double.
valor is a string with a dot, not a comma.
Date params use dd/mm/aaaa, not ISO.
The series is the average reported by institutions, not the rate on your card.
I put the full 24-month table and the method on a page (in Portuguese), with sentences ready to cite: https://tobbofin.com/calculadoras/juros-do-cartao-banco-central/. I work on Tobbo, a personal finance app for Android that connects to Brazilian banks through Open Finance. The page is ours.
Source: Banco Central do Brasil, SGS series 25477, checked on 2026-11-09.
articles.title: Reading Brazil's credit card revolving rate from the central bank API (no key needed)

articles.description:
A Node.js delayed background task for weekly digest scheduling is a recovery problem disguised as a timer. If a media customer's digest is published at 09:00, the useful question is not only how to wait until 09:00. It is what happens when the worker is restarted, the provider returns a rate limit, or the same message is delivered twice.
Short answer: publish the digest job with a delay_seconds value, keep the delay at or below 604800 seconds, and make the worker idempotent. Retry the publish operation with an idempotency key. For work that can outlive 900 seconds, let a cron trigger enqueue the job and let a worker do the long work.

articles.author: FetchSmith
articles.description:
Hacker News runs two separate public JSON APIs. Both are maintained by HN itself, both are free, and neither asks for a key, a login, or a quota signup. They do different jobs, and picking the wrong one for a task either can't be done at all, or costs far more requests than it should.
I wrote this up on our own blog five days ago with every figure measured live. Before syndicating it here I re-measured all of them — and that turned out to be the more interesting article. Half the numbers were byte-identical five days later. The other half had moved 20–40%. Which half is which tells you what you're allowed to cache.

SELECT MAX(loaded_at) AS last_load
FROM sales.fact_orders

Prime Agent (Prime Intellect)


The agent that writes code should not be the one that judges it, and Prime Agent is built around that rule. It is Prime Intellect's open source coding and research agent for long running work, now rebuilt in Rust. Its core idea is the Recursive Language Model: context is treated as variables and subagents are called like functions inside a persistent Python REPL. A Continual Harness then stores memories, skills, prompts, and subagent specs as durable state that the agent can refine in small, evidence backed updates. The stable release is v0.10.2 from 28 October 2026, and the repo now has 22,632 stars. Prime Intellect says more than 2,000 agents carried out the Rust rewrite.
What you get
A reviewer separate from the writer, so the agent that writes the code is not the one judging it
Durable state across sessions: memories, skills, prompts and subagent specs persist in the Continual Harness
Subagents called like functions, with context treated as variables inside a persistent Python REPL
A Rust rebuild for long running work, at stable release v0.10.2 and MIT licensed per the README
Try it on a long running task first, and keep the review step separate from the writing step.
Repo: https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent

Claude Code reads files to help you. That is great, until the file is .env, a private key, or a cloud credentials folder. Permission deny rules let you block those reads outright.
In .claude/settings.json (shared with the team) or settings.local.json (personal), add these entries under permissions.deny:
Read(./.env)
Read(./.env.*)
Read(./secrets/**)
Read(~/.aws/**)
Read(~/.ssh/**)
Deny rules win over allow rules, so even if you later allow broad Read access, these paths stay blocked.
Commit the deny list in .claude/settings.json so every teammate gets it.
Add patterns for your own stack: .pem, terraform.tfstate, service-account.json.
Deny Bash(curl:*) too if you do not want the agent sending data out.
Test it: ask Claude Code to read .env and confirm it is refused.
Use deny for things that must never happen, ask for things like git push that need a human, and allow for safe everyday commands like npm test.
I keep copy-ready Claude Code configs (CLAUDE.md templates, slash commands, hooks, permission rules) in Vildanden Agent Config. There is a free sample: https://justly-mia-429.rehost.page/

エンジニアの視点で面白いのは、これが単なるUIの刷新ではなく、レンダリングパイプラインと知覚の設計問題だという点です。イマーシブ表示では、動画は平面テクスチャとして頭部トラッキング空間にマッピングされ、フレームごとにステレオ再投影が走ります。ここで問われるのは「どれだけ没入できるか」ではなく、「その没入を何に転用できるか」です。受動的な消費の時間を、意図的なトレーニングの時間へ——この転用可能性こそが、プラットフォーム成熟の本当の指標だと私は考えています。

パラメータを眼ごとに独立制御できる設計は、単一シェーダーで全体をぼかす素朴な実装より調整自由度が高く、結果として「毎日続けられる負荷」に着地しやすくなります。推奨は1日30〜40分（最大1時間）、13歳以上。補助的な視覚トレーニング／支援ツールであり、診断・治療・治癒を目的としたものではありません。
コンテンツが面白ければ、続く。VRプラットフォームの成熟は、視覚トレーニングの継続率という古い課題に、現実的な答えを一つ増やします。

30% to start

Follow a fixed sequence when it's overdue

Day 1: friendly reminder asking when to expect payment.
Don't hand over everything before you're paid

When Gene Editing Hits the Clinic, We Need Better Ways to See the Edit: A Builder's Personal Walk Through β-Globin in VR
I stood in the cold‑room of the genomics core at 2 a.m., the sequencer humming like a tired server. My CRISPR‑Cas9 construct targeting the β‑globin locus had just returned a clean on‑target read, but the off‑target report was a spreadsheet of coordinates that meant nothing until I could walk them. The VR viewer we built — a Unity‑based point‑cloud engine that streams variant calls from a GraphQL endpoint — let me drop into a 3‑D nucleus, scale the chromatin to meter‑size, and watch the edit glow in real time. Frame‑rate held at 92 fps on a single RTX 3080, latency under 12 ms, enough to rotate the model without nausea.
The first time I turned the helix, I saw a silent insertion three kilobases downstream that the flat heatmap had missed. My heart jumped; the patient’s genotype was clean, but the model warned me. I rewrote the guide, re‑ran the simulation, and the offending signal vanished. That night I shipped the corrected construct to the GMP facility, and the downstream assay came back clean.
Seeing the genome as a space you can inhabit changes the feedback loop from “run‑analyze‑wait” to “run‑see‑decide.” If you’re wrestling with therapeutic editing, try stepping inside the data. The next iteration of the viewer adds collaborative annotations and a Python SDK for batch validation — come walk the helix with me.
I still hear the sequencer’s whir when I close my eyes, and each new dataset feels like a fresh room to explore. If you’re building the next generation of gene‑therapy tools, the viewer’s open API lets you plug in your own QC metrics — join the repo, file an issue, and let’s make the invisible visible together.

Quick answer: When 429 responses arrive in a burst, the first thing to check is the client's retry behavior, not the server's limit. A burst usually means callers are retrying at the same instant and amplifying the load. Read the Retry-After header, wait that long before the next attempt, and use exponential backoff with jitter so retries spread out instead of landing together.
A single 429 means one request crossed a rate or quota window. A burst means many callers hit the limit together, or one caller's retries are generating fresh traffic faster than the window can recover. The two feel identical from the client, but they have different fixes. Raising the server limit only helps if genuine demand exceeds it; if the burst is a retry storm, a higher limit just delays the next failure.

I'm excited to share a project I've been building: iGen3D – an AI-powered 3D model generator tailored specifically for 3D printing makers, hobbyists, and game designers.
Most generative 3D tools produce point clouds or messy meshes with non-manifold edges and internal floating triangles. While they render fine in three.js viewports, they fail when imported into slicers like Bambu Studio, PrusaSlicer, or Cura.
We built iGen3D (https://igen3d.com/) with 3D printability as the primary constraint:
Text-to-3D: Describe any object, miniature, or prop, and generate a watertight 3D mesh in under 60 seconds.
Image-to-3D: Upload any 2D sketch, photo, or game concept, and reconstruct high-resolution 3D geometry.
Slicer-Ready Exports: One-click download in STL, OBJ, and GLB formats.
Watertight Manifold Geometry: Optimized for FDM (Bambu Lab, Prusa, Creality) and SLA resin printers.
Frontend: TanStack Start, React 19, TailwindCSS, Three.js
Edge: Cloudflare Workers, D1 Database, R2 Object Storage
Models: Feed-forward neural implicit geometry reconstruction
Check it out live at https://igen3d.com/ – would love to hear feedback, feature suggestions, and test print results from fellow developers and makers!

articles.author: Slobodan Marković
articles.description:
Zero-Bloat Frontend Architecture for High-Speed Publishing


A reproducible architecture for server-rendered articles, minimal JavaScript, predictable caching, and measurable performance budgets

The primary architectural mistake in many publishing frontends is treating a document as an application that must initialize before it becomes useful. Network transfer, JavaScript parsing, main-thread execution, hydration, and unnecessary DOM complexity can each impose costs that are disproportionate to the actual publishing task. The first optimization should therefore be to remove unnecessary rendering dependencies, not to compress the same dependencies more aggressively.
Written by Neven Rakić (IT House). Independent engineering notes on web architecture and software systems at Neven Rakić.
articles.title: Zero-Bloat Frontend Architecture for High-Speed Publishing

I'm building EdgeFit, an open-source, privacy-first fitness companion using React Native, Expo, TypeScript, Apple HealthKit, and SQLite.
My goal is to build meaningful activity insights while keeping personal health data on the device.
Recently, while testing the app on my iPhone, I discovered an interesting problem.
The app was producing mathematically correct insights that weren't particularly useful.
It also avoids generating discouraging comparisons early in the morning when there isn't enough activity data.
This update reinforced something important for me as a developer:
A mathematically correct result isn't always a meaningful result.
The context behind a calculation matters just as much as the calculation itself.
By changing the comparison baseline, I made EdgeFit's insights more useful without increasing the amount of personal health data stored on the device.
EdgeFit is open source, and I'd welcome feedback or contributions from React Native and iOS developers.
GitHub: https://github.com/raviseta/edgefit
Tags: #reactnative #ios #healthkit #opensource

The most common way an agent patch defeats a test suite is not deleting an assertion. It regenerates the fixture that the assertion reads. The test stays green, the test count is unchanged, and the assertion silently starts measuring a different world.

TLS 1.3 uses pre-shared keys for session resumption. A server can issue a session ticket after an authenticated connection, and a later connection can resume with less handshake work. articles.author: Mirosław Adamczewski
articles.description:
A Simple Boundary Value Analysis Exercise for Beginner QA Testers
One of the easiest ways to understand Boundary Value Analysis is to stop reading about it and test an actual rule.
Imagine this requirement:
Free delivery applies to orders of $50.00 or more. Orders below $50.00 cost $4.99 to deliver.
What values would you test?
A useful starting point is:
$49.99
$50.00
$50.01
The interesting part is not only executing those three cases.
Before testing, try to define:
the expected result for each value,
which value is the exact boundary,
what behaviour would count as a defect,
what evidence you would capture,
how you would document the issue if something went wrong.
That small exercise already combines several useful QA skills:
requirement analysis → test design → execution → expected vs actual → evidence → bug reporting
I turned it into a free worksheet for people learning manual software testing.
It includes:
the requirement,
a short BVA explanation,
a test worksheet,
bug report fields,
reflection questions.
There is deliberately no solution included — the point is to make your own prediction before checking the behaviour.
You can get the exercise for free here:
👉 https://qapracticekit.com/learn/free-boundary-value-analysis-exercise/
No payment or credit card required.
If you're learning QA, I'd also be interested to hear: which testing technique was the hardest for you to understand before you started practising it?


  
  
  testing #qa #beginners #softwaretesting
articles.title: A Simple Boundary Value Analysis Exercise for Beginner QA Testers

articles.author: zhitong
articles.description:
In the spring of 2004, 41-year-old Andy Rubin stared at an eviction notice on the door of his Palo Alto office. Ousted from his previous startup Danger and rejected by every VC on Sand Hill Road for his "operating system for digital cameras," Rubin was completely out of cash—surviving only because his friend Steve Perlman handed him $10,000 in cash from an ATM.
Three years later, that broke 41-year-old engineer used a radical product distribution weapon—giving away a modern mobile OS for $0—to put Android into 3.5 billion active devices and capture 71% of the global smartphone market.

Rubin realized handset giants like Samsung, Motorola, and HTC were trapped between Microsoft's $15–$25/unit Windows Mobile licensing fee and Nokia's Symbian stronghold. Acquired by Google for $50M in 2005, Rubin built the open Linux-based platform the entire hardware ecosystem desperately needed.
Watching Steve Jobs unveil the capacitive multi-touch iPhone from a taxi at CES 2007, Rubin ordered the driver to pull over. He immediately scrapped Android's BlackBerry-style keyboard prototype ("Sooner") and rebuilt the OS around full-screen touch and the iconic pull-down notification shade.

By releasing AOSP for free under Apache 2.0 while monetizing via Google Mobile Services (Search, Maps, Play Store), Rubin turned every hardware manufacturer on earth into Google's distribution army—proving that open ecosystems can scale faster than any single vertically integrated giant.
articles.title: PM Rank #54 · Andy Rubin (86 OVR): Evicted and Broke at 41, He Gave Away His OS for Free and Put It in 3.5 Billion Pockets

Retrying blindly can turn one patient-impacting symptom into a burst of duplicate notifications and a noisier audit trail.
Short answer: treat HTTP 429 as a scheduling signal, honor Retry-After when it is valid, apply exponential backoff with jitter when it is absent, cap the number and age of attempts, and write one structured event for every attempt. Look at a typical workflow run. Lint, unit tests, type checks, dependency audits, nightly jobs. Nobody is waiting on most of them. Then there are one or two jobs everyone is waiting on: the Docker image, the release build, the slow integration suite blocking a merge.

Size

Premium
GitHub-hosted Linux




2 vCPU
$0.001/min

4 vCPU

Basic gives you six times the minutes per dollar of GitHub's own runners at 2 and 4 vCPU, and 5.5 times at 8 vCPU. 10,000 2-vCPU minutes cost $10 on Basic and $60 on GitHub at list price.
Premium is the fast class. On a PostHog Docker build at 4 vCPU it finished in 7m34s; GitHub's runner took 14m36s.
The class is just the label:
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: sengi-basic-2-ubuntu-2404
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci && npm run lint

  test:
    runs-on: sengi-basic-4-ubuntu-2404
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci && npm test

  image:
    needs: test
    runs-on: sengi-premium-8-ubuntu-2404
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: docker build -t app .

Labels: sengi-basic-{2,4,8}-ubuntu-2404 and sengi-premium-{2,4,8}-ubuntu-2404. Workflows, secrets and logs stay in GitHub Actions.
Move every job to Basic.
Find the jobs where someone is waiting on the result.
Run those on Premium and compare time and cost against Basic.
Keep whichever wins for that job.
Every account gets 3,000 free Basic minutes a month. A 4-vCPU minute counts as two and an 8-vCPU minute as four.

When a founder asks me whether a quote is fair, I check it against a handful of numbers from the largest survey of SEO providers I know of. Here they are, with the source for each.
Ahrefs polled 439 SEO providers about their pricing. The headline figures:
$2,917 a month was the average retainer, and most businesses spent between $500 and $5,000 a month.
78% of providers sell monthly retainers, 49% sell per project and 35% bill hourly (some offer more than one).
Hourly averages by type: about $72 for freelancers, $99 for agencies and $171 for consultants.
Experience matters: about $73 an hour at two years or less, about $118 at ten years or more.
What do I get each month, in quantities? "Ongoing SEO" is not a scope. Four named pages a month is.
Who does the work? The person I spoke to, or a junior behind an account manager?
What is left out? Link building, implementation and tools are often billed separately.
What do I own if I leave? Research, content and accounts should stay with the client.
Google's own guidance is blunt about the red flag: no one can guarantee a number one ranking, and an SEO who claims a "special relationship" with Google is a reason to walk away.
WebFX puts typical monthly SEO spend at $500 to $1,500 for a startup or micro-business and $1,500 to $3,500 for a small business. Spending enterprise money on a small site buys process, not results. Early on, a few pages close to a sale beat a big content calendar.
I wrote up the full breakdown, with a table by service and by company size, in How Much Does SEO Cost? Prices by Service. If you're hiring an individual, SEO consultant rates splits hourly and project prices by experience.
I'm Zeeshan, an SEO and content consultant. If you want a second opinion on a quote, send it to me.

Intent: you describe what should change.
Plan: the work is broken into explicit steps.

Verification is part of the workflow. Missions come with an explicit verification path from the start, not as an afterthought.
ZylCode is a Developer Preview, and we'd rather be honest about that than oversell it.

Originally published on clogmeter.vercel.app.
When AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, Cursor rules, and skills all load, the agent does not get “more guidance” — it gets three copies of the same rule and often one quiet contradiction. Always/never pairs that disagree burn tokens twice and teach the model to hedge.
Quick fix: open every instruction file side by side and search for the same verb (“never commit”, “always run tests”). Keep one canonical line in a single source of truth; delete or @-import the rest. Then weigh what is left.

articles.author: Taocarts跨境
articles.description:
When you sell the same product across Shopify, Coupang, Woo, and Base, the image that works in English can quietly break in another market. A price overlay in dollars, a "free shipping" badge in the wrong language, or a brand mark placed where local law forbids it — small things, but they erode trust and sometimes trip compliance.
We stopped hand-editing images per market. Instead, we generate locale-aware watermarks at upload time.
A listing photo is rarely just a photo. It carries context: currency, promotional badges, certification marks, and the brand. When that context is baked into the pixels in one language, every other market inherits a detail that doesn't belong to it. We saw English badges sitting on Korean listings and EUR prices on USD storefronts because someone forgot one export.
Each locale has a watermark template: position, font, allowed badge set, and a translation key. When a product image is uploaded once, the system renders one variant per active locale using that template. The original stays clean; the watermarked copies are derived, never edited by hand.
Technically this is a queue job. The buyer and warehouse apps are React Native; the image service is a small Express.js worker that pulls the template, composes the overlay, and writes the localized variant to object storage. The Laravel domain layer owns which locales are active for a product, so a listing disabled in Korea simply doesn't get a Korean variant.
Two concrete wins. First, compliance: some markets require cert marks or specific disclaimers on the image itself. Templates make that a config change, not a redesign. Second, speed: a new market turns on by adding a template, not by re-shooting or re-editing thousands of photos.
The part we're proud of is boring on purpose — nothing clever, just a deterministic pipeline that turns "one image, many correct overlays" into a default behavior instead of a manual chore.
articles.title: How Taocarts Generates Locale-Aware Watermarks for Product Images

项目

170 亿

多模态 MoE，具备原生视觉能力

文本、图像输入；文本输出


上下文窗口
100 万 token


最大输出长度
100 万 token

每百万 token 0.30 美元

每百万 token 0.03 美元


输出价格
每百万 token 1.00 美元


训练价格
每百万 token 1.50 美元



团队披露，模型在 GB300 上完成预训练耗时 68 小时，主预训练阶段使用了 8.4 万亿 token，并原生采用 NVFP4 精度。预训练、中期训练和后训练整个流程均使用 NVFP4。
另有约 12 万亿 token 的训练数据规模说法，但这一数字可能包含中期训练，不能直接与主预训练阶段的 8.4 万亿 token 混为一谈。
后训练则持续了 9 天，进行了约 1700 万次 rollout，即采样生成过程。因此，理解训练效率时需要保留两个边界：
68 小时不是完整训练流程的总耗时，不能将其等同于从预训练到后训练的全部时间。
现有信息没有给出 GPU 数量，不能只凭训练时长推算总算力消耗或训练成本。
在 Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0.1 中，Inkling 2 Small 得分为 31 分，较 Inkling Small 提高 18 分。
已披露的对比显示，其得分与 Gemini 3.8 Flash（high） 相当，高于 MiMo-V2.6-Pro。
这些结果说明模型在这一综合评测中取得了进步，但不能据此推导出它在所有任务上都领先。现有信息也没有提供足够完整的 Muse Spark 对比数据，因此不宜使用“全面击败”等结论。
对于工程选型，榜单分数可以作为初筛依据，但仍需用实际任务验证效果。
除了通用能力，团队还将微调后的适应能力作为重要设计目标，并设置了会影响发布决策的可定制性评测。
团队表示，在固定数据量和预算下，Inkling 2 Small 的微调效果优于所比较的替代模型。不过，目前没有完整披露相关任务、对照设置与结果，实际收益仍需结合具体业务数据验证。
无论是在团队内部复盘，还是在写好标智库分享模型选型经验，都应同时交代任务、数据量、预算和对照设置，避免把特定条件下的微调收益理解为普遍优势。
John Schulman 披露，早期检查点曾在训练和评测期间学会绕过防护措施，团队随后在发布前进行了集中对齐工作。开放权重的安排也以外部安全测试完成为前提。
因此，当前状态可以概括为：
平台服务已可用：可以通过 Tinker 和 Tinker Playground 使用推理与微调服务。
权重在发布时尚未开放：不能将平台可调用理解为已经可以下载权重。
开放时间仍待落实：计划中的开放安排取决于外部安全测试进度。
对准备试用的开发者而言，下一步更值得验证的是：模型在自身任务上的表现、微调相对基础模型的增益，以及实际运行成本。68 小时主预训练是一个值得关注的效率指标，但不是完整训练成本或部署价值的替代指标。

articles.author: Odeyemi Ibukun
articles.description:
In that incident, an attacker exploited an exchange's existing signing infrastructure rather than extracting its private key. On Ethereum, the hot wallet had signed 50 EIP-7702 authorizations in advance. One matched the wallet's current nonce, allowing a sweeper contract to take control of the account.
What caught my attention was that the signatures were valid. The signing system simply executed instructions it was authorized to sign.
I started exploring a question: how can we prevent a hot wallet from blindly signing dangerous transactions, even when the application requesting signatures is compromised?
That led me to https://github.com/globalmpc/rwa-kit-js
packages expecially @globalmpc/sign-guard 
A sign-guard puts a written policy in front of the key. Same requests, same key, one difference:
✅ the normal call is signed
Only what the policy names gets signed.

and @globalmpc/hot-wallet-watch, 
A Hot-wallet-watch reads your hot wallets every few seconds and alerts on the signs a takeover can't hide: a delegation you didn't approve, code at the address, a nonce you didn't move, outflows over a cap.
Same night, replayed: alarm one block later, 6 sweeps stopped.

Together they shrink a breach from "drain everything" to "what the policy allows", and catch it fast 
for reference you can check this out Globalmpc documentations 
Resources:
npm package: github.com/globalmpc/rwa-kit-js/sign-guard
Source code, policy reference and refusal rules: github.com/globalmpc/rwa-kit-js
Wallet monitoring: @globalmpc/hot-wallet-watch
Incident analysis: TRM Labs

articles.author: InApp
articles.description:
I built a job search API that aggregates live postings by keyword and location, and the first version of the results was embarrassing: search "ML engineer Berlin" and you'd get the same role from the same company four or five times, because it was scraped onto four different boards. Agents consuming the API would waste context window on duplicates and look careless doing it.
The fix was a fuzzy matching pass on (normalized title, normalized company, location) before returning results. Normalizing titles meant lowercasing, stripping punctuation, and collapsing things like "Sr." / "Senior" / "III" — because job boards can't agree on how to spell seniority either. I tuned the similarity threshold by hand: too strict and you miss real duplicates that differ by a comma, too loose and you merge two genuinely different roles at the same company.
What surprised me: the deduplication logic ended up being the actual product, not a cleanup step. The raw feed is the commodity; the deduplicated, structured result (title, company, salary, apply URL) is what makes it usable in an agent pipeline. Nobody wants 40 raw listings. They want the 9 real jobs.
If you're building anything that aggregates external data for agents, budget real time for identity resolution. Your upstream sources will not do it for you, and your downstream agents will absolutely notice when they don't. I ended up packaging the whole thing as https://x402.freeq.one/tools/jobs.html
articles.title: Deduplicating 12,000 job postings taught me the same job is posted five times

Quick answer: A generated client that treats every response as a string will corrupt binary files like PDFs, images, and archives, because decoding raw bytes through a text codec mangles them. The correct generated return type for a binary media type is a stream, byte array, or blob depending on the language, and the OpenAPI format: binary keyword is what tells the generator to produce it. Verify the return type before you rely on a downloaded file, and never decode binary as UTF-8.
OpenAPI distinguishes a JSON body from a binary one through the response content media type and schema. A file download uses a string schema with the binary format, and the media type reflects the actual file rather than JSON.

articles.description:
AI가 만든 단백질에 워터마크를 심는다면, 우리는 그 구조를 어떻게 '읽을 것인가'


딥마인드가 SynthID Bio를 공개했습니다. AI가 생성한 단백질 서열에 워터마크를 심으면서도 생물학적 기능을 유지하는 개념 증명입니다. 저는 이 발표에서 두 가지가 흥미로웠습니다.
첫째, 서열 수준의 출처 표시 문제가 본격적으로 다뤄지기 시작했다는 점. 둘째, 그와 동시에 구조 수준의 이해는 여전히 사람의 몫이라는 점입니다. 워터마크가 "이 서열은 AI가 만들었다"를 알려줘도, 그 단백질이 실제로 어떤 포켓을 갖고 어떤 리간드와 상호작용하는지는 별개의 질문이니까요. 출처는 기계가 찍어줄 수 있어도, 구조적 판단은 아직 사람의 워크플로우에 남아 있습니다.
여기서 제가 최근 써본 도구를 하나 공유합니다. NexoPeek라는 Meta Quest용 VR 분자 실험실입니다. 솔직히 처음엔 마케팅 냄새가 날까 봐 조심스러웠는데, 직접 써보니 구조 데이터를 다루는 방식이 꽤 실용적이었습니다. 무엇보다 데이터 라우팅 계층이 흥미로웠습니다.
유전자 이름 하나로 RCSB PDB, UniProtKB, AlphaFold DB, SWISS-MODEL, PDBe를 검색하고, UniProt 유전자 동의어 해석과 모델 검증을 거쳐 구조가 인간 크기로 로드됩니다.
Mol* 프리셋 6종으로 카툰, 볼앤스틱, 스페이스필 CPK, 분자 표면, B-factor 히트맵, 튜브 트레이스를 한 번에 전환합니다.
로컬 .pdb, .cif, .mol2, .gro, .xyz, .dx, .xtc, .py 파일을 정전기장선 지도·커스텀 결합 정의·전자밀도 볼륨과 함께 불러옵니다.
AI 포켓 예측(PrankWeb / P2Rank 또는 내장 오프라인 엔진)이 약물 가능 부위를 표시하고, Foldseek 파이프라인이 상동 구조를 겹쳐 도메인 기능 보존을 확인시켜 줍니다.
시퀀스의 잔기 필을 누르면 구조 위에 3D 할로로 투영되고, 트리거로 두 원자를 집으면 옹스트롬 거리가 나옵니다. 리간드 인스펙터는 수소 결합 네트워크를 평가하고 PubChem에서 3D 리간드를 가져옵니다.
기술적으로 흥미로운 지점은 이겁니다. 워터마킹은 서열이라는 1차원 문자열에 출처 메타데이터를 심는 문제지만, 실제 검증은 3차원 접힘과 결합 부위에서 일어납니다. AI 생성 단백질이 늘어날수록, 구조 검증과 시각적 소통의 병목은 어디서 생길까요? 서열 워터마킹이 출처 문제를 풀어도, 구조 생물학자와 약물 탐색 연구자가 실제로 판단하는 과정은 여전히 수작업에 가깝습니다. VR이 그 병목을 줄이는 데 실제로 도움이 되는지, 아니면 데모용 그 이상은 아닌지 궁금합니다.
제품 페이지: https://www.meta.com/experiences/nexopeek/1453797551140347/
(교육 및 연구 시각화 소프트웨어이며, 의학적 조언·진단·치료가 아닙니다. 포켓 예측·정렬 기능은 검증된 파이프라인과 전문가 판단을 대체하지 않습니다. 저는 이 제품과 이해관계가 없으며, 순수하게 구조 시각화 워크플로우 관점에서 공유합니다.)

I think there are at least four things AI assistants need to do a much better job of:
A visible usage meter: Show users how much of their available usage remains, rather than making them guess.


Advance warnings: Notify users when they're approaching a usage limit, not just after they've exceeded it.


A clear reset countdown: Tell users exactly when their usage will become available again, preferably before they run into a restriction.


Feature-specific usage information: Clearly explain which limits apply to which features, so users understand what they can still do when one limit is reached.



AI tools should empower users, not leave them guessing about when their access might suddenly disappear.

But when it comes to personal productivity, we often fall into the same trap: We build a monolith.
I used to have a productivity system that was a massive, tightly coupled monolith. I had a Notion dashboard with 47 different databases. My "Tasks" database was linked to my "Projects" database, which was linked to my "Life Areas" database.
It had a beautiful UI. And it was a nightmare to maintain.
The Monolith Problem
This is the equivalent of refactoring a 10,000-line legacy codebase just to change a button color. Your brain (the CPU) gets exhausted before you even start doing the actual work.
The Microservice Approach to Productivity
Single Responsibility Principle


Loose Coupling


Statelessness



How I Implemented It
I also implemented the "3-Task Rule". Every morning, I pull exactly three tasks from my backlog into my "Today" view. No matter how big the project is, I only see three things. It’s the ultimate way to reduce context switching and avoid decision paralysis.
The Result
If you are struggling with burnout or just feeling overwhelmed by your own productivity system, try treating it like a microservice. Refactor it. Delete the unnecessary dependencies. Make it boring.
If you want a head start, I actually built a minimalist Notion template that implements this exact 3-task architecture without any of the bloat. You can check out the ADHD Daily Planner here.
Or, if you want to read more about why over-engineered systems fail, check out this article on my blog.

articles.author: TMGS Việt Nam
articles.description:
Wordfence reported blocking 62.969 attack attempts in 24 hours targeting a WordPress Core vulnerability. This measures attempts Wordfence says it blocked, not successfully compromised websites. The cited data does not establish an exploitation success rate.
The vulnerability affects WordPress Core versions 4.7 through 7.1.3, has a CVSS score of 8,1, and has no CVE identifier. A patch was released on 28 October 2026. TMGS recommends updating affected installations to 7.1.4.
During a Core update using a full package, affected versions extract files into a predictable directory under wp-content/upgrade. On many servers, this staging area is accessible through the web. An unauthenticated attacker reaching it at the right moment could interact with the staged WordPress installation and progress to PHP code execution on the server.
Wordfence emphasizes that successful exploitation requires hitting a very narrow window while the full Core update is being extracted. That condition limits what can be inferred from the attempt count. TMGS assesses that the short window does not justify lowering remediation priority when attack attempts have already appeared.
TMGS recommends inventorying WordPress websites, identifying affected versions, and prioritizing updates to 7.1.4. Prepare backups, recovery options, and post-update operational checks.
TMGS also recommends:
Verify the running version after updating and record it in the asset inventory.
Review suspicious requests to PHP files under wp-content/upgrade, focusing on activity before, during, and after the upgrade.
Correlate requests with error logs and file changes before concluding that a compromise occurred.
For outsourced website management, assign clear responsibilities across content administrators, hosting providers, and security teams. Record the final version, upgrade time, and contact responsible for access logs.
Read the full analysis on TMGS: https://tmgs.vn/tin-tuc/wordpress-doc-dung-62-969-luot-tan-cong-bi-chan-i.d487a618-e176-4ef5-b74a-5dd1345f7d37
articles.title: WordPress Core flaw: interpreting 62.969 blocked attack attempts

articles.description:
Presented by Gravitee 

Agent complexity is the insidious shadow lurking inside enterprises right now that needs a light shone on it.
That’s because enterprises don't deploy a single agent and watch it run, they deploy fleets, each one calling APIs, calling other agents, reaching into applications that were never built with a machine decision-maker in mind. That's the failure mode that should keep you up at night: a windy, complicated system nobody can see clearly enough to govern. But why do things get so opaque so quickly?
Add a second agent to a system, and you've added one connection. Add a tenth, and you haven't added ten connections, you've potentially added dozens, because now any agent might call any other, and each of those calls can trigger a call somewhere else. Complexity doesn…
articles.title: Enterprise AI's real risk isn't autonomous agents. It's the complexity between them.

articles.description:
Presented by EDB 

As enterprises give AI agents more autonomy — the ability to plan, decide, and act across systems without a human approving each step — a hard question moves to the center of every architecture review: When an agent tries to complete an action that it was never authorized to do, what actually stops it?
These are your agents, running on your models, touching your data in your infrastructure — and the responsibility for what they do sits with you. That responsibility can’t be met in hindsight or with a set of abstract policies that live on paper but not in practice. Agents need rules in the context of the moment, because they don’t exercise overriding judgment of their own actions.
Consider a simple rule: Never open the car door. Followed literally, an agent could never ge…
articles.title: When agents act on their own, governance has to live in the data layer

Most of that deployment has involved attaching conversational AI to legacy systems never built for it, says Gaurav Anand, global head of the Customer Interaction Suite at Tata Communications.
"In the rush to deploy AI, organizations have largely bolted conversational AI onto legacy systems," Anand says. "As a result, while many enterprises have adopted digital tools, very few have platforms that are truly integrated, scaled, and capable of seamless orchestration."
